newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says political muscle the crux of EMU success.
newsitem.headline: EMI says political muscle the crux of EMU success.

text.p: Europe's embryonic central bank has thrown down the gauntlet to the continent's politicians, saying monetary strategists have done all they can to ensure the euro's planned launch in 1999 is a success.

With inflation levels now reassuringly low throughout Europe, state leaders must complete the picture with sound recipes for budgetary restraint and structural reform, the European Monetary Institute (EMI) urged on Tuesday.

"The stability-oriented monetary policies followed now by all the EU central banks are here to stay," EMI President Alexandre Lamfalussy declared, as he applauded the swift evolution of low inflation rates Europe-wide.

Meanwhile, as budget deficits continue to run unacceptably high amid record joblessness, the chances for a successful move to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) "will depend on how governments plan their future policies," the EMI chief said.
Analysts said on Wednesday that his comments betrayed a rising concern that a lack of political ability to push through reforms could disrupt the central bankers' efforts to push for a strong euro.

"Central bankers can't run a one-legged race, they need help," said Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber. "The EMI has got the remit it wants for the ECB -- independence and a clear commitment to price stability -- but that is not a lot of use if governments go off on a fiscal bender."

Data published in the EMI's annual report showed European Union debt positions in 1996 far exceeding the three percent deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) and sixty percent debt-to-GDP reference levels set down in the Maastricht Treaty.
Lamfalussy was quick to stress that these data did not constitute a forecast for 1997, on the basis of which the EMU starting group will be selected in early 1998.
Nonetheless he castigated governments for failing to cut their deficits further and said the EMI was "not entirely happy" with the revenue-driven ways cuts had been achieved.

Lamfalussy's key demand is that attempts to cut state deficits "should be the outcome of a basic reform package," and not rely on boosting revenue by one-off measures, a charge once levelled at France over its now-sanctioned use of pension fund transfers from France Telecom.

In a broadly predictable contrast to politicians, many of whose careers hinge on a successful euro start, Lamfalussy also refused to say a 1999 launch was a certainty and instead said the chance was "significantly more than 50 percent".

"The EMI may be getting a little bit nervous," said Bank Julius Baer European economist Adrian Owens. "On the one hand EMU has to go ahead on time, yet there are more fiscal convergence problems now than might have been expected a year ago. I think the EMI was trying to strike a balance between going after politicians and not really scaring investors."

Owens and others say the EMI, which will file a recommendation on the choice of the EMU starting group along with the European Commmission, has also given a stong hint that it will not brook any fiscal lightweights taking part in the launch of the single currency, even if they meet the initial entry conditions.

Asked what the Maastricht Treaty debt criteria meant to him, Lamfalussy stressed that they had three aspects: the reference levels, the leeway for some divergence, and the importance of sustainability of the levels reached.

That is good news for economic powerhouses like France and Germany, which despite recent hiccups have an overall strong reputation for stability and budgetary control, but bad news for the "Club Med" countries, whose record is less glowing.

"What the EMI is really saying is that all threes (percent) are not the same. Only those with a proven track record are going to form the core group," said PaineWebber's Cottrell, refering to the three percent to GDP deficit target.
Cottrell noted that while central bankers in theory will not directly influence the final choice of EMU participants, their viewpoint will still be crucial.

"Heads of state are going to take notice. I can't imagine that (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl will try to push something through parliament while the Bundesbank is in the background saying: No, no, no," she said.
But others said the EMU selection process was still seen as likely to involve a degree of compromise.

"In an ideal world, the EMI may really want deepseated structural reforms throughout Europe but in practice they will probably have to settle for less. They will have to be pragmatic," said Julius Baer's Owens.
